Acute Appendicitis: The patient presents with acute hypogastric pain and nausea, and the examination reveals localized tenderness in the right lower abdomen and hypogastrium with a positive McBurney’s sign and rebound tenderness. The laboratory studies show a white-cell count of 19,000/μL, which is consistent with acute appendicitis. The CT scan demonstrates an abnormally low transverse colon and right colic flexure, with small-bowel loops clustered above and to the right, and an abnormal superior mesenteric artery-vein relationship, which are also consistent with acute appendicitis. The diagnostic differences between acute appendicitis and other candidate diseases, such as gynecological disorders, inflammatory bowel disease, and mesenteric ischemia, support the diagnosis of acute appendicitis.
Mesenteric Ischemia: The patient presents with acute hypogastric pain and nausea, and the examination reveals localized tenderness in the right lower abdomen and hypogastrium with a positive McBurney’s sign and rebound tenderness. The CT scan demonstrates mesenteric congestion and prominent vessels, which are consistent with mesenteric ischemia. The abnormal superior mesenteric artery-vein relationship on the CT scan also supports the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia. However, the presence of a normal appendix on the CT scan and the absence of bowel infarction make acute appendicitis a more likely diagnosis. The diagnostic differences between mesenteric ischemia and other candidate diseases, such as gynecological disorders and inflammatory bowel disease, support the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia as a possible alternative.
